title: Mandela Effect
summary: The Mandela Effect is a vivid example of how *collective* memory can diverge from the historical record. It illustrates that memory is better understood as a **reconstruction** process shaped by attention, expectation, and social context, rather than as a simple recording of the past.

content_html:
Mandela Effect

The Mandela Effect is a term used to describe situations where large numbers of people remember an event or detail differently from how it is recorded in historical documents or other reliable sources. The name comes from many people reporting that they clearly remember Nelson Mandela dying in prison in the 1980s, even though he was actually released, became president of South Africa, and died in 2013.

  • It involves shared false memories, not just one person misremembering.
  • People often report the memories as being very vivid and certain, which makes the discrepancy surprising.
  • Common examples include remembered spellings, logos, or movie lines that do not match the historical record (for example, many people recall the line as “Luke, I am your father,” while the actual line in The Empire Strikes Back is “No, I am your father”).

Most psychologists explain the Mandela Effect using normal memory processes:

  • Memory is reconstructive: each time we recall something, we rebuild it, which can introduce small errors.
  • Social reinforcement: when we talk to others who share a similar inaccurate memory, we become more confident that it is true.
  • Source confusion: we mix details from different sources (films, news, conversations) and misattribute where a particular detail came from.
